newsitem.title: USA: MBS market yawns ahead of June producer price data.
newsitem.headline: MBS market yawns ahead of June producer price data.

text.p: Action in the mortgage-backed securities market was subdued on Thursday ahead of the June Producer Price Index (PPI) report on Friday, sources said.

The overall June PPI, according to economists surveyed by Reuters, was expected to remain unchanged, while the so-called core PPI was seen increasing by 0.1 percent. Core PPI excludes the volatile food and energy components.
A New York-based trader said he saw some strength in the 8.0-percent coupon, however, that firmer tone was seen as more of a correction from weakness in prices experienced earlier in the week.
One New York interest-only (IO) security trader recalled that this session saw a single bond out for the bid. That inverse IO was said to have come from an account in California.
"In our opinion, it traded very well," said the trader, noting that while the session was quiet, the IO transaction did not make market waves.
Earlier, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp announced that 30-year mortgage commitment rates declined 15 basis points to an average 7.47 percent in the latest week.

Mortgages, said one market observer, have softened in the wake of a decline in interest rates and, in the near-term, their performance was expected to be muted until "a reasonable back-up in rates" materialized.

The market obsever added that the lower rates were having some impact and that it would take an uptick in the 10-year Treasury note yield to 6.50 percent before mortgage investors felt comfortable. Even with a 6.50-percent T-note, investors would feel jittery, the market observer said.

Much of the anxiety hinged on expectations that lower rates would inspire a spate of homeowner refinancings and early mortgage securities prepayments. That concern about prepayment risk had already been acknowledged by some players.

According to a recent report published by Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, Merrill's fixed income market watchers recommended defensive strategies within mortgages to reduce exposure to so-called negative convexity or price compression.

"In particular, the relatively small spread-widening necessary for mortgages to underperform Treasuries suggests that investors are not being adequately compensated for risk inherent in a market that has outperformed all year," according to the report.
Indeed, there has been some talk among investors of a move into Treasuries as a result of this prepayment risk.

The concern about lower interest rates and heightened prepayment activity has prompted some market participants to talk of a retreat out of current and cusp coupons and a move into lower coupons. But, one buysider contended that such a move may provide a buying opportunity for those investors who do not expect the U.S. economy or inflation to overheat.

Among key issues, Government National Mortgage Association 7.5 percent 30-year bonds declined 3/32 to 101-8/32 bid to a bond equivalent yield of 7.35 percent. Comparable Federal National Mortgage Association securities declined 1/32 to 101-02/32 while Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. securities also fell 1/32, to 101-07/32.
Ten-year Treasury notes were unchanged at 102-22/32 to yield 6.25 percent and the 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged at 100-25/32 for 6.56 percent yield.
